2. Facts are given by my brother and it is not necessary to detail them. Suffice it to say that the respondent Matiar Rahman who was the Executive Engineer. Buildings-Electrical Division of the Ministry of Public Works and Rural Development failed to submit the estimate in time in compliance with the orders of the Superintending Engineer. He, however submitted the estimate on 9th May, 1974 through the Superintending Engineer by his order dated 6th December, 1973 asked him to submit necessary estimate immediately. The allegation is that instead of taking up the works he wrote to the Superintending Engineer to forward a copy of administrative approval of the proposed construction. Exception was taken for such step and a departmental proceeding was drawn up as to why he should not be dismissed from service or otherwise suitably punished for inefficiency and misconduct within the meanings of clauses (a) and (b) of rule 3 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976. The explanation was not satisfactory and inquiry was held. The Inquiry Officer found him guilty of failure to submit the estimate in time and recommended a minor punishment of censure. The Government, however, decided to award the extreme punishment and a second show cause notice was issued. Thereafter the matter was referred to the Public Service Commission seeking its advice as to whether the extreme punishment of dismissal should be imposed upon the respondent. The Public Service Commission gave advice that dismissal would be harsh and opined that censure would meet the ends of justice in this case. The Secretary to the Ministry concerned, however, took the view that the officer "acted deliberately to sabotage order of his superior". It was further found that "it was a case of deliberate disobedience and calls for stringent punishment for gross misconduct". Accordingly, the Secretary suggested that the officer may be dismissed from Government service. The matter was placed before the President and the President ordered the dismissal of the respondent. The High Court Division declared the order of dismissal as illegal since no reason for higher punishment was assigned. 

 3. The factual aspect of this case is that the respondent officer was asked to submit an estimate in November 1973 by the Superintending Engineer. In turn he asked whether there has been any Government approval. Thereafter no further reminder was given nor the respondent officer was asked to submit his estimate. Thereafter everybody kept quiet, However in May '74 the respondent submitted his estimate. Then in July he was given show cause notice for misconduct. The respondent officer stated that………….. 

 Commencing the Electrical work on 31.5.74 I completed the case simultaneously with completion of the building construction work. There was no delay in the connection of the Electrical works. As such there was no complaint from any corner for the Electrical works. 

 So the question of misconduct within the meaning of clause (b) of rule 3 of Bangladesh Government Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) rules can hardly arise," 

 In this background the question was whether misconduct had really been proved. The Inquiry Officer recommended minor penalty namely, censure but the Government decided to impose a major penalty. Opinion of the Public Service Commission was obtained. It expressed the opinion that the dismissal would be harsh in the facts and circumstances of the case and recommended censure but the Secretary took a strong view and suggested dismissal. It is true that the Government is not bound by the opinion of the Public Service Commission but certainly it being a Constitutional authority its opinion demands a careful consideration. The facts of the case could at the most demonstrate a certain amount of extra caution on the part of the respondent officer or peevishness at the worst. The question is whether any case was made out for passing the order of dismissal ignoring the recommendation of both the Inquiry Officers and the Public Services Commission. The Secretary in his note used very strong words namely, "sabotage" "disobedience," "deliberate disobedience," etc. It is unfortunate, that he has gone to the length of saying "such disobedience which led to the pecuniary Loss on the part of the Government," which, however, was never made a matter of charge against the respondent officer. The charge is Annexure "C" to the Writ Petition. It does not say a word about pecuniary loss on the part of the Government. The statement of allegation states that the officer was directed to take up the work in an expeditious way and submit the estimate. And the allegation states: 

 4. As for the view that has been taken by my brother, Shahahuddin Ahmed, J that if in a particular case the punishment awarded is harsh or unreasonable the Court may interfere thereof to meet the ends of justice and the view has been taken that the punishment of dismissal in this ease is harsh and, therefore, it has been suggested that it should be reduced to compulsory retirement. Once judicial mind has oscillated on the question of punishment and the harshness has become apparent, the only decision that is called for is to say whether the punishment is contrary to the recommendation of Public Service Commission was illegal or without lawful authority or not. The respondent has not filed the petition in mitigation of sentence. He has challenged the very decision on the ground of illegality and arbitrariness It is not enough that the authority has been vested with a power and the authority concerned has been satisfied in what way the power has to be exercised, When there are categories of penalty—minor penalty and major penalties—and there are as many as four types of minor penalties, and four types of major penalties, the question of imposition of punishment becomes relevant for consideration as to the application of mind of the authority concerned. The authority concerned must assign some reasons white awarding a particular type of penalty. So, that when challenged it can be demonstrated that the penalty imposed is commensurate with the charge proved. That the dismissal is harsh runs like a refrain of this else. The enquiry officer recommended censure.' The Public Service Commission opined that the dismissal will be harsh and censure will be enough. Even the ultimate Judicial view is such, e.g. punishment by dismissal is harsh and it should be compulsory retirement which again is a major penalty yet the respondent it seems cannot get the relief for which he came before the Court of law. To my mind the charge proved calls for a minor punishment, namely, censure or withholding of promotion for a specified period. It is interesting that Rule 4(2) (d) provides for recovery from pay of the whole or in part of any pecuniary loss caused to Government by negligence or breach of orders. In this case though the Secretary has harped on the theme of pecuniary loss without having any basis for it, the recovery of such loss is consigned as a minor penalty and assuming the Secretary is correct, which however is not borne by facts, still on his own showing it calls for a minor penalty by law. Instead dismissal was passed which is a major penalty and the suggested compulsory retirement in the judgment of my learned brother is also a major penalty. In this view of the matter I would dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the High Court Division. No cost. 

 Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—Government of Bangladesh is the appellant in this appeal by special leave. It is directed against an order of the High Court Division dated April 3, 1981 in Writ Petition No. 572 of 1980 declaring null and void the appellant's order dated July 22, 1977 dismissing the respondent from the service on grounds of inefficiency and misconduct under the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976. 

 6. Respondent Matiur Rahman was an Executive Engineer, Buildings-Electrical Division of the Ministry of Public Works and Rural development at the relevant time. His immediate superior, the Superintending Engineer, by the written order asked him to take up the electrical works of the building’s for accommodation of 14 Ministers of State with their secretaries in the Jatiya Sangsad Building at Tejgaon, Dacca before the next session of the Jatiya Sangsad and to submit the necessary estimate immediately so that the works could he completed before the en-suing sessions of the National Assembly. The respondent received this order on 6 December, 1973, but instead of taking tip the work he wrote to the Superintending Engineer to forward a copy of the administrative approval of the proposed construction along with an abstract showing the provision of electrical installation in connection with the proposed work at an early date for estimation purpose. No such copy was sent to him; he, however, submitted the estimate on 9 May, 1974. The President's Vigilance and Inspection Team; in the course of supervision of the electrical works of the building, made adverse comments on the Executive Engineer's failure to submit the estimate in time in compliance with the order of the Superintending Engineer. Following these adverse remarks, the Government drew a departmental proceeding against the respondent and by an order dated 19 July, 1976 asked him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service or otherwise suitably punished for 'inefficiency' and 'misconduct' within the meanings of clauses (a) and (b) of Rule 3 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976, herein-after referred to as the 'Rules.' The respondent submitted his explanation contending that the delay in submitting the estimate did not constitute the offences of inefficiency or misconduct and that the alleged delay was due to confusion as to whether he should proceed with the work without waiting for a copy of the administrative approval which was sought for from the Superintending Engineer. The Government not being satisfied with this explanation appointed the Deputy Chief Engineer to inquire into the matter. An inquiry was accordingly held on the conclusion of which the Inquiry Officer submitted a report holding the respondent guilty of failure to submit the estimate in time and recommending a minor punishment or 'censure.' The Government accepted the finding that the respondent was guilty but did not accept the recommendation for minor punishment; the Government provisionally decided to award the extreme punishment of dismissal from service, and for that purpose issued a second show-cause notice dated 12 April, 1977 as to why the proposed punishment should not be imposed on him. The respondent showed cause against the proposed punishment by a letter in which he repeated his previous stand that he was not guilty of any offence. The Government then referred the matter to the Public Service Commission seeking its advice as to whether the extreme punishment of dismissal should be imposed upon the respondent. The Public Service Commission gave advice that 'dismissal' would be harsh and that 'censure' would meet the ends of justice in this case. But the Government did not accept the advice of the Public Service Commission, and by the impugned order dated 22 July, 1977, dismissed the respondent from service. 

 7. Respondent challenged the legality as well as the propriety of this order of dismissal by filing the writ petition as already referred to, contending that the recommendation of the Enquiry Officer and the advice of the Public Service Commission in favour of minor punishment were binding upon the Government. The High Court Division, as appears, did not express any clear opinion as to the advice of the Public Service Commission, but rejected the respondent's contention that recommendation of the Enquiry Officer was binding upon the Government. The High Court Division also rejected the respondent's contention that his failure to submit the estimate in time did not constitute the offence of inefficiency or misconduct and found that the charges brought against the respondent were established. But the High Court Division relying upon a decision of this Division in the case of M. A. Hai Vs. Trading Corporation of Bangladesh. 32 DLR (AD) 46 observed that when the Enquiry Officer recommended a minor punishment but the appointing authority, namely the Government in this case, decides to impose a higher penalty the appointing authority was required to assign reasons for awarding the higher punishment. In this view of the matter the High Court Division declared the impugned order of dismissal illegal since no reason for giving the higher punishment was assigned. 

 8. Leave was granted to consider the questions whether the recommendation of the Enquiry Officer appointed under Rule 10 of the Rules in respect of punishment is binding upon the "authority"; whether the advice of the Public Service Commission in this regard, if any, given under Rule 7(6) of the Rules is binding upon the Government while inflicting a higher punishment than the one recommended by the Enquiry Officer; and whether the High Court Division properly appreciated the decision of this Division in the case of. M.A. Hai Vs. Trading Corporation, 32 DLR (AD) 46. 

 9. We have heard at considerable length both Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the appellant and Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel for the respondent on these points. We find that there is no provision in the Rules requiring the Enquiry Officer to give any recommendation as to the punishment to be imposed while submitting his report of enquiry held by him under these Rules. What he is required to do is to submit a "report of his findings'' to the authority" by whom he was appointed: and the latter is required by these Rules to consider the report and record its findings on the charge". These provisions of the Rules show that the 'authority', which may be government itself, is not bound to accept the findings of the Enquiry Officer not to speak of his recommendation, but may come to a different finding on the basis of the materials on record. The authority may also direct 'further enquiry' either by the same officer or by another officer. As to recommendation for punishment, since the enquiry officer is not required by the Rules to make recommendation the authority is not bound to accept such recommendation even if given. But though not required to recommend any punishment, the enquiry officer while submitted his report finding a government servant 'guilty' ordinarily expresses Opinion as to the punishment which he considers to be suitable or appropriate in the case, The authority may accept such a recommendation but it will not be correct to say that it is bound to do so, It is for the authority to initiate as well as to dispose of a departmental proceeding, and the roles of the Enquiry Officer is only to help the "authority" in making at a correct and impartial finding on the charges leveled against the delinquent officer, It is, therefore quite natural that the 'authority' is the sole judge as to what punishment should be awarded. 

 10. As to 'advice' of the Public Service Commission, such advice may be given only in a case "in which consultation with a Public Service Commission is necessary Advice of the Public Service Commission is necessary if the authority is of the opinion that the penalty of removal of dismissal from service should be imposed. When an advice is sought by making a reference to the Public Service Commission, advice may or may not be given and the case shall be disposed of by the authority in accordance with the procedure as quoted below: 

 "If such advice is tendered within twenty days of receipt of the proceedings by the commission, the authority shall consider it and pass appropriate orders on the case. But if no such advice is tendered within that period, the authority may, on the expiry of that period, pass appropriate orders on the case". 

 11. As to the next question whether the impugned punishment of dismissal is a nullity for not assigning any reasons, we find that the view taken by the High Court Division is based on an appreciation made by this Division in the case of Abdul Hai Vs. Trading Corporation 32 DLR (AD) 46, The observation is quoted below: 

 This Division did not opine there that failure to assign any reason for higher punishment would render the order of punishment null and void, but in the facts of that case It observed that the "authority is expected to assign some reasons." It was a case concerning an employee of a statutory Corporation where terms and conditions of services of its employees were not regulated by any statutory rules. However, an employee of such Corporation is entitled to an opportunity to show-cause against any proposed punishment following the principles of natural justice. In the case of a government servant,' whose terms and conditions of service are regulated by the service rules, he is entitled to a show-cause notice even for the second time after a finding against him is provisionally recorded and a specific punishment is proposed to be awarded to him. In this case the respondent was served with a second show-cause notice as to why he should not be dismissed and accordingly he submitted a lengthy explanation not only against the proposed higher punishment but also against the findings of the Inquiry Officer. Secondly, the higher punishment was imposed with the approval of the President of the Republic to whom his case was forwarded by the Secretary of the Ministry concerned, In his forwarding note, dated 13 July, 1977 the Secretary stated the reasons for awarding the higher punishment which are that the failure of the respondent to comply with the urgent order of the superior officer in time was deliberate and estimate was not submitted in spite of reminders. We are, therefore, unable to accept the view of the High Court Division that the imposition of the higher punishment was without any lawful authority. 

 12. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Counsel for the respondent, in view of these difficulties, tried to defend the impugned order of the High Court Division on a new ground altogether. Mr. Ahmed has contended that the respondent was punished for an offence for which he was not charged. The basis of this contention is the 'forwarding note' of the Secretary of the Ministry to the President the copy of which is Annexure '3' of the Supplementary affidavit-in-opposition on Behalf of the Government in the Writ Petition No. 572 of 1980. There the Secretary mentioned the expressions "disobedience," "deliberate disobedience" "flouting the order" meaning that the respondent was guilty of disobedience although he was not charged for "disobedience" but he was punished for disobedience. Respondent was not charged for "disobedience" simply because disobedience" has not been used in the Rules as an offence There "misconduct" has been stated to be one of the offences for which a government servant may be punished. "Misconduct" means conduct prejudicial to good order or service discipline or unbecoming an officer or gentleman "Disobedience" as mentioned in the forwarding note fits in the definition of 'misconduct' Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed then contends that the respondent did not disobey his superior officer's order. It is true that he did not straightaway disobey the order saying that he would not obey it, but willful omission to comply with the order also amounts to disobedience. It is argued that the respondent in fact complied with the order after writing for a copy of the order of administrative approval and that he was not responsible for the delay. But it has been found by the enquiry officer that the respondent was reminded of the order for taking up the work both by the Superintending Engineer and the Assistant Engineer and that when the superior officer passed the order to take up the work the respondent was not justified in delaying the work on any plea. The respondent had his office in the same building in which other concerned officers also held office as such, be could have got the matter clarified if he bad the intention to take up the work in right earnest. Delay of six months in submitting the estimate is found to have been rightly held to be "failure to comply with the order". As such the offence of misconduct was established. Even if, for the sate of argument it is hold that the delay in submitting the estimate does not constitute 'misconduct', it certainly constitutes "inefficiency" for which major penalty of `removal' from service may be awarded as laid down in clause (b) of sub-rule 5 of rule 4 of the Rules. All the contentions of the learned Counsel thus fail. 

 13. The respondent having been found guilty of inefficiency and misconduct, the punishment of dismissal is not illegal. In Writ jurisdiction the question of quantum of punishment is not ordinarily considered. But if in a particular case the punishment awarded is found harsh or unreasonably severe in consideration of the nature of the charges, the court may interfere therewith for the ends of justice. The impugned punishment of dismissal in this case is considered to be harsh. We, therefore reduce it to that of compulsory retirement within the meaning or clause (b) of sub-rule (3) of Rule 4 of the Rules. With this modification, the appeal is allowed, the order of the High Court Division is set aside and the Writ Petition is dismissed. No order as to costs.
